# The Standard Error {.title-left}

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## You'll learn to

::: presenter-space
- Explain what the **standard error** of a slope measures.
- Connect it to the idea of **repeated sampling**.
- Distinguish the standard error from the **standard deviation**.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Starting point: a regression from a sample

::: presenter-space
- We regress **ideology** (0–10 scale) on **age** using the British Election Study.
- Slope: 0.017 per year of age. Older respondents lean slightly more right.
- This estimate comes from one particular sample of 2,649 respondents.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## This estimate depends on our sample

::: presenter-space
- If the BES had surveyed different people, the slope would differ slightly.
- Our estimate of 0.017 is **one of many possible outcomes**.
- How much would the slope vary across different samples?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The thought experiment: many samples

::: presenter-space
- Imagine drawing 10 new surveys of the same size.
- Each yields a slightly different slope: 0.019, 0.015, 0.021, 0.014, 0.018...
- The estimate varies from sample to sample.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The sampling distribution of the slope

::: presenter-space
- If we drew thousands of samples, the slopes would form a **distribution**.
- This is the **sampling distribution** of the slope.
- It is centred on the true population slope.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The standard error is the SD of this distribution

::: presenter-space
- The **standard deviation** measures spread in observed data.
- The **standard error** measures spread in estimated slopes across samples.
- Same concept, different target: data vs. estimates.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why this matters for inference

::: presenter-space
- A small SE means the slope is **precisely estimated** (similar across samples).
- A large SE means the slope is **imprecisely estimated** (varies a lot).
- The SE is what makes p-values and confidence intervals possible.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Reading the standard error in regression output

::: presenter-space
|  | Coefficient | Std. err. |
|---|---|---|
| **Age** | 0.017 | 0.002 |
| **Intercept** | 3.84 | 0.114 |

- Each coefficient has its own standard error. 
- The ratio coefficient/SE is the t-statistic.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The t-statistic: how many SEs from zero?

::: presenter-space
- The **t-statistic** is the slope divided by its standard error: $t = b / SE$.
- It asks: how far is the estimate from zero, measured in standard errors?
- A large $|t|$ (roughly above 2) means the slope is unlikely to be zero by chance.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Recap

::: presenter-space
- The **standard error** measures how much a slope would vary across repeated samples.
- Smaller SE means a more precise estimate.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

::: presenter-space
**Why this matters:**

- Every regression estimate comes from a single sample.
- The standard error quantifies the uncertainty in that estimate.
- Understanding SE is essential for interpreting significance and confidence intervals.
:::
